findings.reason: The protected function is compact, conventional expert-interview code. It isolates February's only year-dependent rule, gives the leap predicate an immediate semantic name, and uses a fixed set for the four 30-day months. The valid-month contract makes the final 31-day branch exhaustive; a candidate would add no material correctness, clarity, robustness, or maintainability benefit.

For February, the predicate accepts every year divisible by 400 and otherwise exactly years divisible by 4 but not 100, separating ordinary leap years, exceptional leap centuries, ordinary years, and non-400 centuries. For valid non-February inputs, membership in {4, 6, 9, 11} returns 30 exactly for the four shorter months and the fallback returns 31 for the remaining seven. All 6216 legal year/month pairs matched calendar.monthrange.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode algorithm problem 1118, Python/Python 3, and Solution.numberOfDays. Authenticated source evidence confirms the year and month inputs, integer month-length result, three exact examples, and the closed constraints 1583 through 2100 and 1 through 12.

The protected solve body and immutable native method bound to verified submission 2067722513 have identical executable statements: the same February branch, Gregorian leap expression, 29/28 choice, fixed 30-day-month set, and 30/31 choice. Their only differences are the app function versus native class wrapper, native annotations, and app module docstring.

Following the original-18 blocker playbook, the package retains its verified bounded_domain certificate rather than fabricating scaling over twelve month classifications. The certificate binds lc_1118 to O(1), records a positive source-derived bound of 12, and supplies bounded-work and exhaustive-domain evidence. The app real-test passed with runtime_check false, zero tiers, complexity_check true, and method bounded_domain; the calendar oracle, protected function, native method, and table control agreed on all 6216 legal pairs.

The Approach accurately derives the necessary and sufficient Gregorian leap predicate, the 400-year and 100-year exceptions, the four 30-day months, and the exhaustive final month class. Its O(1) time and O(1) space explanation matches the branch manifest, certificate, and implementation, and it covers table/library alternatives, both common leap-rule mistakes, February classes, 30-day months, and boundary years.

The modular Reference preserves the source's concise request, all three exact examples without invented explanations, both exact constraints, and both hints in order. Its independent contract explains month numbering, ordinary month lengths, and the complete leap rule needed to interpret the requested calendar result.

A fresh authenticated review verified three examples with no explanations, two constraints, two hints, and no tables, images, diagrams, notes, or follow-up. source_fidelity.json binds every composed local section to live statement hash a14c0a867dd856cb2b25590ac94ed4c611bf6c830ed6c2333fd022a075e7b021.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly three examples and no explanations. The first three cases preserve their year, month, and output literals in source order: an ordinary 31-day month, a leap century divisible by 400, and a non-leap century divisible by 100 but not 400.

All nine ordinary fixtures are visible samples or trials. They cover every executable branch: non-century leap February, ordinary February, a 30-day month, a 31-day month, both year bounds, both month bounds, a 400-divisible century, and a 100-divisible non-400 century.

An independent oracle uses Python's calendar.monthrange, while a separately structured control starts from a twelve-entry ordinary-year month table and adjusts February only for a leap year. Neither shares the protected function's branch-and-set layout.

The oracle, protected app-local function, immutable native Solution method, and table control agreed on all nine authored cases and every one of the 6216 legal pairs formed by years 1583 through 2100 and months 1 through 12.

The package intentionally has no benchmark.json. Its unchanged bounded_domain certificate replaces scaling with a fixed-work proof and exhaustive-domain check; direct validation confirms its required O(1) bound, workload maximum 12, and both mandated replacement-check kinds.

The app real-test selected nine correctness cases and zero performance cases, passed every case, reported no runtime check or scaling points, and identified a passing bounded_domain certificate instead of a measured runtime verdict.
